metadata.scope: e_britannia (all baronies across k_ireland and k_scotland)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding (stripped of key prefixes and parenthetical notes).
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier extracted from modern_name; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.anachronism_type: Mutually exclusive historicity category: attested_pre_867 | fictional_placeholder | post_867_eponym | renamed_post_867 | modern_anachronism | early_modern_foundation | high_late_medieval_attestation | unattested_indigenous_or_minor.
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= that bookmark year.
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation for the audited name (negative values = BCE; null if unattested).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.eponym: Structured eponym object {year, post_867, type, details} when named after a person, saint, ruler, deity, or dynasty/tribe; null otherwise.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.historical_names: List of distinct pre-867 attested names for the same site or immediate predecessor: [{name, native_script, language, attested_from, attested_to, source, relationship, notes}].
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_dromahair.first_mention_attestation: O'Rourke stronghold built c. 950 AD; earlier site known as Drumlease (5th c. Patrician foundation).
b_dromahair.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Droim Dhá Ethiar (modern Droim Dhá Thiar), 'ridge of the two (air) demons', referring to the ridge above the River Bonet.

historical_names.name: Drumlease
historical_names.source: 5th-century Patrician church foundation of Drumlease (Droim Lias) on the same ridge.
historical_names.notes: The ridge was known as Drumlease (Droim Lias) from the 5th to 10th centuries before Dromahair emerged as the O'Rourke capital of Breifne.

historical_names.name: Droim Lias
historical_names.source: 5th-century Patrician church foundation of Drumlease (Droim Lias) on the same ridge.
historical_names.notes: The ridge was known as Drumlease (Droim Lias) from the 5th to 10th centuries before Dromahair emerged as the O'Rourke capital of Breifne.

b_belcoo.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Seamus Pender's 'A Census of Ireland, Circa 1659' as 'Belcow'; the Ulster Cycle tale 'Togail Bruidne Bélchon Bréifne' is Middle Irish (post-867).
b_belcoo.etymology_analysis: From Irish Béal Cú, either 'mouth of the narrow [stretch of water]' between Upper and Lower Lough MacNean, or folk-etymologized from the Ulster Cycle warrior Bélchú of Breifne.

b_longford.first_mention_attestation: Dominican priory founded at Longford in 1400; attested as 'An Senlongport' in the Annals of Ulster (1430) and 'Longford-O-ffeargail' (1448).
b_longford.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish An Longfort (earlier Longphort Uí Fhearghail, 'stronghold of O'Farrell'), from Old Irish longphort (ultimately Latin longus + portus).

b_cavan.first_mention_attestation: Founded between 1300 and 1330 by Giolla Íosa Ruadh O'Reilly, Lord of East Breifne.
b_cavan.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish An Cabhán, 'the hollow', describing the low-lying basin where the O'Reillys established their town and friary in the early 14th century.

b_adragh.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 or medieval attestation found for 'Adragh' in Breifne; possibly a CK3 spelling of Ardagh (Co. Longford) or the minor townland Adragh (Co. Monaghan).
b_adragh.etymology_analysis: Unattested as a baronial settlement by 867 AD; likely reflects either Irish Áth Darach ('ford of oaks') or a metathesized form of Ardagh (Ardachadh, 'high field').

b_galway.first_mention_attestation: Annals of the Four Masters (1124): erection of the castle/fortress of Dún Bhun na Gaillimhe by Tairrdelbach Ua Conchobair, King of Connacht.
b_galway.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Gaillimh (from Dún Bhun na Gaillimhe, 'fort at the mouth of the Gaillimh'), named after the River Gaillimh (now the Corrib), meaning 'stony river'.

b_athenry.first_mention_attestation: Athenry Castle built before 1240 by Meyler de Bermingham; First Battle of Athenry recorded in 1249 (Annals of Loch Cé / AFM).
b_athenry.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Baile Átha an Rí (earlier Áth na Ríogh, 'ford of the kings'), referring to a crossing on the Clarin River in the territory of the Soghan kings.

b_tuam.first_mention_attestation: Monastic foundation of St. Jarlath in the 6th century; attested in early Irish annals as Tuaim Dá Ghualann.
b_tuam.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Tuaim (earlier Tuaim Dá Ghualann, 'burial mound of two shoulders'), cognate with Latin tumulus, referring to an ancient burial mound.

b_da_chainoc.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical settlement name in Connacht; no pre-867 or medieval documentary record found.
b_da_chainoc.etymology_analysis: Appears to be an Old Irish saintly hypocoristic name (Da-Chainnóc, 'my little Cainnech'), but unattested as a documented settlement in Connacht.

b_cruachu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Crúachu / Crúachan in Tírechán's 7th-century Collectanea (Book of Armagh) and Félire Óengusso (c. 800).
b_cruachu.etymology_analysis: Old Irish Crúachu (genitive Crúachan, modern Ráth Cruachan / Rathcroghan), the traditional royal capital of Connacht, derived from Old Irish crúach ('mound, hill').

b_castlebar.first_mention_attestation: Developed around a castle built by the Anglo-Norman de Barra (Barry) family by 1235.

eponym.details: Named after the Anglo-Norman de Barra (Barry) family, who built a castle there c. 1235.

b_castlebar.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Caisleán an Bharraigh ('Barry's Castle'), named for the 13th-century Anglo-Norman de Barra stronghold on the Castlebar River.

b_sligo.first_mention_attestation: River Sligeach listed among Ireland's seven 'royal rivers' in the 9th-century tale 'Togail Bruidne Da Derga' (settlement later attested in Annals of Ulster 1188).
b_sligo.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Sligeach ('abounding in shells'), originally the name of the Garavogue River estuary due to its rich shellfish beds and shell middens.

b_killala.first_mention_attestation: 5th-century Patrician foundation (Cell Alaid) placed under St. Muredach; attested in early ecclesiastical records.
b_killala.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Cill Ala (Old Irish Cell Alaid), 'the mottled/speckled church', an early Patrician episcopal foundation in north Mayo.

b_wexford.first_mention_attestation: Old Norse Veisafjǫrðr (Middle English Weiseforthe, 12th c.) emerged from the Viking trading settlement (9th–10th c.); earlier Gaelic name Loch Garman.
b_wexford.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Veisafjǫrðr ('inlet of the mudflats') via Yola/Middle English Weiseforthe, replacing the older Irish name Loch Garman.

historical_names.name: Loch Garman
historical_names.source: Early Irish dindsenchas tradition for Loch Garman ('lake of Garman').
historical_names.notes: Loch Garman is the pre-Norse Irish name of the harbour and settlement before the Viking name Veisafjǫrðr/Wexford.

b_enniscorthy.first_mention_attestation: Enniscorthy Castle built c. 1205 by the Anglo-Norman de Prendergast family.
b_enniscorthy.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Inis Córthaidh, 'island of Corthaidh' or 'island of rocks', situated on the River Slaney.

b_ferns.first_mention_attestation: Monastery founded in 598 AD dedicated to St. Aidan/Mogue (Fearna Mór Maedhóg); attested in early Irish annals.
b_ferns.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Fearna (short for Fearna Mór Maedhóg), meaning 'alder-grove', seat of a major 6th-century monastery and the Kings of Leinster.

b_carlow.first_mention_attestation: Anglo-Norman Carlow Castle built c. 1207–1213 by William Marshal; made a borough in 1296.
b_carlow.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Ceatharlach (historically Caherlagh/Caterlagh), likely from Old Irish cethrae ('cattle, herds') + -lach ('place of cattle'), though folk-etymologized as Ceatharloch ('four lakes').

b_gowran.first_mention_attestation: Attested in early Irish annals and Leinster/Osraige texts as Gabrán / Bealach Gabráin (eastern boundary of Osraige).

morphemes.translation: place of goats or personal name Gabrán

b_gowran.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Gabhrán (anciently Bealach Ghabhráin, 'Gabrán's pass'), a pre-Norman royal residence of the Kings of Ossory.

b_kilkenny.first_mention_attestation: First recorded as 'Ceall-Cainnigh' in the Annals of the Four Masters for 1085 (before then, the district/capital was known as Osraighe).
b_kilkenny.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Cill Chainnigh ('church of St. Cainnech/Canice'), named after the 6th-century abbot St. Cainnech of Aghaboe; first attested as a place-name in 1085.

b_athy.first_mention_attestation: Developed from a 12th-century Anglo-Norman settlement and crossing on the River Barrow.
b_athy.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Baile Átha Í ('town of the ford of Ae'), named after a legendary 2nd-century chieftain killed at the River Barrow crossing.

b_carrick.first_mention_attestation: Earliest known record of Carrick-on-Suir (Carrig Mac Griffin) is a 1247 charter of fairs granted to Matthew Fitzgriffin.
b_carrick.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Carraig (Carraig na Siúire, 'rock of the Suir'), an Anglo-Norman island settlement on the River Suir.

b_athlone.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the annals in 1001 when Brian Boru sailed his army up the Shannon to Athlone.
b_athlone.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Baile Átha Luain ('town of Luan's ford'), a strategic crossing on the River Shannon south of Lough Ree.

b_birr.first_mention_attestation: 6th-century monastery founded by St. Brendan of Birr; Synod of Birr held in 697 AD (Cáin Adomnáin).

morphemes.translation: watery place, plain of water, watercress

b_birr.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Biorra ('plain of water' or 'watery place'), an ancient monastic centre in Éile.

b_uisneach.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Annals of Ulster (516, 714 AD) and Tírechán's 7th-century Collectanea as Uisnech.

morphemes.translation: place of the hearth/cinders or angular place

b_uisneach.etymology_analysis: Old Irish Uisnech (modern Uisneach), the sacred central hill of Ireland, derived by Eric Hamp from Proto-Celtic *us-tin-ako- ('place of cinders/hearth').

b_dublin.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Annals of Ulster (841/842 AD) as Duiblinn (Viking longphort), alongside earlier Áth Cliath.
b_dublin.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Middle Irish Duiblinn ('black pool'), referring to the dark tidal pool at the confluence of the Poddle and Liffey.

historical_names.name: Áth Cliath
historical_names.source: Early Irish annals and hagiography (Áth Cliath 'ford of hurdles' and Duiblinn 'black pool' both attested <= 867 AD).
historical_names.notes: Áth Cliath (Baile Átha Cliath) was the pre-Viking Gaelic ford settlement alongside the ecclesiastical/tidal-pool site of Duiblinn.

historical_names.name: Dubh Linn
historical_names.source: Early Irish annals and hagiography (Áth Cliath 'ford of hurdles' and Duiblinn 'black pool' both attested <= 867 AD).
historical_names.notes: Áth Cliath (Baile Átha Cliath) was the pre-Viking Gaelic ford settlement alongside the ecclesiastical/tidal-pool site of Duiblinn.

b_wicklow.first_mention_attestation: Anglo-Norman/late 12th-century records as Wykinglo (from Old Norse Víkingaló).
b_wicklow.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Víkingaló ('Vikings' meadow') via Middle English Wykinglo, distinct from the Irish name Cill Mhantáin.

b_kildare.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the late 5th/early 6th century by St. Brigid as Cill Dara; attested in Cogitosus's 7th-century Life of Brigid and Annals of Ulster.
b_kildare.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Cill Dara ('church of the oak'), named for the oak tree beside which St. Brigid established her 5th-century monastery.

b_trim.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Áth Truimm in the Book of Armagh (c. 807), recording the 5th-century church founded by St. Lommán.
b_trim.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Old Irish Áth Truimm (modern Baile Átha Troim), 'ford of the elder trees', on the River Boyne.

b_drogheda.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1194 by Anglo-Norman lord Hugh de Lacy.
b_drogheda.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Droichead Átha ('bridge at the ford'), referring to the bridge across the River Boyne.

b_tralee.first_mention_attestation: Founded by the Anglo-Normans in the early 13th century (Earls of Desmond stronghold; Dominican friary 1243).
b_tralee.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Trá Lí (formerly Tráigh Lí), 'strand of the River Lee', at the head of Tralee Bay.

b_cork.first_mention_attestation: 6th/7th-century monastic settlement founded by St. Finbarr; attested in the Annals of Ulster (821, 846 AD) as Corcach.
b_cork.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Corcaigh (Old Irish Corcach, 'marsh'), referring to the marshy island in the River Lee where St. Finbarr founded his monastery.

b_kinsale.first_mention_attestation: Anglo-Norman Baron of Kinsale created c. 1181; Church of St. Multose built 1190; royal charter granted 1334.
b_kinsale.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Cionn tSáile ('head of the brine'), describing its position at the tidal mouth of the River Bandon.

b_baltimore.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1413 in 'The Genealogy of Corca Laidhe'; Dunasead Castle built in the 13th century.
b_baltimore.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Baile an Tí Mhóir ('town of the big house'), referring to the O'Driscoll stronghold of Dún na Séad.

b_ennis.first_mention_attestation: Developed in the 12th/13th century when the O'Briens built Clonroad Fort (1210) on Inis Cluana Rámhfhada.
b_ennis.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Inis (short for Inis Cluana Rámhfhada, 'island of the long rowing meadow') between two channels of the River Fergus.

b_kincora.first_mention_attestation: Royal residence of Brian Boru (born c. 941) and the Dál Cais in the late 10th century; rebuilt 1096 (AFM).
b_kincora.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Ceann Coradh ('head of the weir'), referring to an ancient fishing weir across the Shannon at Killaloe.

b_waterford.first_mention_attestation: Norse city founded in 914 AD as Veðrafjǫrðr (earlier Viking camp 853); earlier Irish name Port Láirge.
b_waterford.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Veðrafjǫrðr ('ram/wether fjord' or 'windy fjord'), adopted in English as Waterford, replacing the Irish name Port Láirge.

historical_names.name: Port Láirge
historical_names.source: Early Irish annalistic and Viking-age tradition (Port Láirge / Loch dá Caech).
historical_names.notes: Port Láirge ('Lárag's port') is the Irish name of the harbour and settlement predating the Old Norse name Veðrafjǫrðr.

b_emly.first_mention_attestation: 6th-century monastery of St. Ailbe; attested in the Annals of Ulster (7th–9th c.) as Imlech Ibuir.

morphemes.translation: border, marshy margin of a lake

b_emly.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Imleach Iubhair ('border of the lake of yews'), an ancient pre-Patrician and Eóganachta ecclesiastical centre.

historical_names.name: Medón Mairtine
historical_names.source: Early Irish historical tradition (capital of the Érainn people of Mairtine).
historical_names.notes: In ancient times the site was known as Medón Mairtine before becoming the chief Eóganachta church of Imlech Ibuir.

b_clonmel.first_mention_attestation: Walled town developed in the 13th century under Anglo-Norman rule (Earls of Ormonde / Otto de Grandison).
b_clonmel.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Cluain Meala ('honey meadow'), referring to the fertile valley along the River Suir.

b_limerick.first_mention_attestation: Old Norse Hlymrekr emerged with the permanent Viking longphort in 922 (earlier Viking raid 812); earlier Irish name Luimneach / Inis Sibhtonn.

morphemes.translation: Norse adaptation of Irish Luimneach ('bare/marshy spot')

b_limerick.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Hlymrekr, an adaptation of Irish Luimneach (originally referring to the Shannon estuary, Loch Luimnigh, and King's Island).

historical_names.name: Luimneach
historical_names.source: Annals recording 812 Viking presence and pre-Viking Irish name Inis Sibhtonn / Loch Luimnigh.
historical_names.notes: Inis Sibhtonn was the pre-Viking Irish name for King's Island, and Luimneach the Irish name for the estuary/site before Norse Hlymrekr.

historical_names.name: Inis Sibhtonn
historical_names.source: Annals recording 812 Viking presence and pre-Viking Irish name Inis Sibhtonn / Loch Luimnigh.
historical_names.notes: Inis Sibhtonn was the pre-Viking Irish name for King's Island, and Luimneach the Irish name for the estuary/site before Norse Hlymrekr.

b_nenagh.first_mention_attestation: Nenagh Castle built c. 1216 by Theobald Walter (Butler family), around which the town grew.
b_nenagh.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish An tAonach (full name Aonach Urmhumhan, 'the Fair of Ormond'), from the traditional East Munster fair held there.

b_roscrea.first_mention_attestation: Monastery founded in the late 6th century by St. Crónán; produced the 8th-century Book of Dimma.
b_roscrea.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Ros Cré ('Cré's wood'), an important early monastic town on the ancient Slighe Dála road.

b_kilmallock.first_mention_attestation: First annalistic notice records a defeat of Waterford Vikings at Cill Mocheallóg in 927 AD (Annals of Inisfallen / AFM).
b_kilmallock.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Cill Mocheallóg ('church of St. Mocheallóg'), named after the 7th-century saint whose church stood on Kilmallock Hill.

b_donegal.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Annals of the Four Masters (1159) and developed as the O'Donnell capital in the 15th century.
b_donegal.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Dún na nGall ('fort of the foreigners'), referring to a Viking encampment at the mouth of the River Eske.

b_raphoe.first_mention_attestation: Annals of Ulster (628 AD) record Cath Botha; 6th/7th-century Columban monastery of Ráth Bhoth associated with St. Adomnán (d. 704).
b_raphoe.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Ráth Bhoth ('fort of the huts'), referring to the monastic cells within an earthen enclosure.

b_fahan.first_mention_attestation: 6th/7th-century monastery founded by St. Mura (Fathain Mura); 7th-century cross-slab survives.
b_fahan.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Fathain Mura ('little green/field of St. Mura'), an early Christian monastery on Lough Swilly.

b_derry.first_mention_attestation: 6th-century Columban monastery; attested as Daire Calgaich in Adomnán's Vita Columbae (c. 700) and Annals of Ulster.
b_derry.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Old Irish Daire (modern Doire), 'oak-grove', originally Daire Calgaich ('oak-grove of Calgach') and later Doire Colmcille.

b_dundalk.first_mention_attestation: First attested as 'Dún Delgain' in the Annals of Ulster for 1002 (earlier accounts call the site simply 'Delga').
b_dundalk.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Dún Dealgan ('fort of Dealga'), adopted by 12th-century Normans at Castletown Mount.

historical_names.name: Delga
historical_names.source: Early Irish Táin Bó Cúailnge / Ulster Cycle tradition ('Delga in Muirtheimne').
historical_names.notes: Early medieval texts refer to the site as Delga/Dealga, with the prefix Dún ('fort') added by 1002.

historical_names.name: Dealga
historical_names.source: Early Irish Táin Bó Cúailnge / Ulster Cycle tradition ('Delga in Muirtheimne').
historical_names.notes: Early medieval texts refer to the site as Delga/Dealga, with the prefix Dún ('fort') added by 1002.

b_armagh.first_mention_attestation: 5th-century Patrician ecclesiastical capital (Ard Mhacha); attested in the Book of Armagh (807) and Annals of Ulster.
b_armagh.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Old Irish Ard Mhacha ('Macha's height'), named after the goddess Macha like nearby Eamhain Mhacha (Navan Fort).

b_ardee.first_mention_attestation: Anglo-Norman town developed from the 13th century (Monastic order of St. John 1207; charter 1378).
b_ardee.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Baile Átha Fhirdhia (earlier Atherdee, from Áth Fhirdia 'ford of Ferdia'), named after the Ulster Cycle duel between Cú Chulainn and Ferdia.

b_clogher.first_mention_attestation: 5th/6th-century episcopal see founded by St. Macartan (d. 506); attested in early Irish annals as Clochar.
b_clogher.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Old Irish Clochar ('stony place'), seat of the ancient kingdom of Airgíalla and the Diocese of Clogher.

b_dungannon.first_mention_attestation: 14th-century castle built by the O'Neill dynasty of Tír Eoghain on Castle Hill.
b_dungannon.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Dún Geanainn ('Geanann's fort'), chief seat of the O'Neills of Tír Eoghain from the 14th century.

b_downpatrick.first_mention_attestation: Earliest extant use of 'Dún Pádraig' / 'Downpatrick' is in Josias Bodley's survey of 1602–1603; earlier known as Dún dá Lethglas / Dún.
b_downpatrick.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Dún Pádraig ('Patrick's fort'), a post-medieval name replacing Dún dá Lethglas / Down.

historical_names.name: Dun da Lethglas
historical_names.source: Annals of Ulster (Dún dá Lethglas) and Ulster Cycle (Ráth Celtchair).
historical_names.notes: Known in the early Middle Ages as Dún dá Lethglas (or Ráth Celtchair) before John de Courcy's 12th-century re-dedication to St. Patrick.

historical_names.name: Rath Celtchair
historical_names.source: Annals of Ulster (Dún dá Lethglas) and Ulster Cycle (Ráth Celtchair).
historical_names.notes: Known in the early Middle Ages as Dún dá Lethglas (or Ráth Celtchair) before John de Courcy's 12th-century re-dedication to St. Patrick.

b_slemish.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 7th-century Patrician hagiography (Muirchú / Book of Armagh) as Sliabh Mis.
b_slemish.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Old Irish Sliabh Mis ('Mis's mountain'), a volcanic plug in County Antrim associated with St. Patrick's captivity.

b_carrickfergus.first_mention_attestation: Carrickfergus Castle built in the late 12th century (c. 1177) by John de Courcy.
b_carrickfergus.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Irish Carraig Fhearghais ('Fergus's rock'), named after Fergus Mór, legendary king of Dál Riata.

b_bangor.first_mention_attestation: Bangor Abbey founded c. 555–558 AD by St. Comgall; attested in early Irish annals as Bennchor.
b_bangor.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Old Irish Bennchor (modern Beannchar), meaning 'place of points' or 'horned curve', referring to the shoreline of Bangor Bay.

b_dundee.first_mention_attestation: Late 12th-century royal charter of William the Lion granting Dundee to his brother David, Earl of Huntingdon (c. 1190); also mentioned in the 12th-century Life of Waltheof for 1054
b_dundee.etymology_analysis: From Gaelic Dùn Dèagh, combining dùn ('fort') with the genitive of a personal name Daig (derived from an Old Celtic root meaning 'fire'). The medieval Latin form Taodunum ('Tay-fort') and Dei donum ('gift of God') are later learned adaptations.

b_kirriemuir.first_mention_attestation: 1249 Taxatio of the Diocese of St Andrews ('vicar of Kerimor')
b_kirriemuir.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic Ceathramh Mhoire, meaning 'quarterland of Mary', referring to an administrative land division dedicated to the Virgin Mary.

b_mar.first_mention_attestation: 1014 Irish annals (unnamed Mormaer of Mar at the Battle of Clontarf); Ruadrí mormar Marr in 1128 and Book of Deer (c. 1131)
b_mar.etymology_analysis: Ancient provincial choronym (Gaelic Màrr) of uncertain origin; proposed derivations include a Brittonic personal name Mar, a cognate of Welsh mawr ('great', cf. Cantref Mawr), or an Old Norse/Celtic root.

b_dunkeld.first_mention_attestation: Annals of Ulster (865 AD: death of Tuathal son of Artgus, primepscop of Fortriu and abbot of Dunkeld)
b_dunkeld.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic Dùn Chailleann ('fort of the Caledonians'), preserving the ancient ethnonym of the Caledonii; early documents record forms such as Duncalden.

b_aberfeldy.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in 1526 as Abrefrally and in 1552 as Abirfeldy
b_aberfeldy.etymology_analysis: From Pictish aber ('river mouth') combined with the stream name Peallaidh (Gaelic Obar Pheallaidh, 'mouth of the Peallaidh'), possibly referring to a water-sprite.

b_dunfermline.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the 11th century (marriage of Malcolm III and St Margaret at Dunfermline in 1070; 'Dunfermelitane' in David I charters of 1128)
b_dunfermline.etymology_analysis: From Gaelic dùn ('fortified hill') combined with an uncertain second element, possibly referring to the Tower Burn or a crooked pool/bend near the Lyne Burn.

b_kircaldy.first_mention_attestation: 1075 grant of the shire of Kirkcaladunt by Malcolm III to the church at Dunfermline
b_kircaldy.etymology_analysis: From Pictish *caer ('fort'), *caled ('hard' or a personal name), and the locative suffix -in ('place of'), meaning 'place of the hard fort' or 'place of Caled's fort'; later influenced by Scots 'kirk'.

b_st_andrews.first_mention_attestation: 12th-century ecclesiastical records (St Andrews / Villa Sancti Andreae replacing earlier Kilrymont)

eponym.details: Named after Saint Andrew the Apostle (1st century AD).

b_st_andrews.etymology_analysis: English/Scots hagiographic name referring to Saint Andrew the Apostle, whose relics were venerated at the cathedral priory; it superseded the earlier Gaelic name Cennrígmonaid / Kilrymont in the High Middle Ages.

historical_names.name: Cennrigmonaid
historical_names.source: Annals of Ulster (747 AD: 'mors Tuathalain abbatis Cinrigh Monai')
historical_names.notes: Cennrigmonaid ('head/promontory of the king's moor') is attested in 747 AD; later Cell Rigmonaid / Kilrymont.

historical_names.name: Kilrymont
historical_names.source: Annals of Ulster (747 AD: 'mors Tuathalain abbatis Cinrigh Monai')
historical_names.notes: Cennrigmonaid ('head/promontory of the king's moor') is attested in 747 AD; later Cell Rigmonaid / Kilrymont.

b_st_johnston.first_mention_attestation: 12th century (colloquial Scots 'St John's Toun' / 'St Johnston' from St John's Kirk, established mid-12th century; Perth itself attested c. 1128)

eponym.details: Named after Saint John the Baptist (1st century AD), patron saint of St John's Kirk.

b_st_johnston.etymology_analysis: Scots hagiographic name ('St John's Toun', contracted to St Johnston) derived from the parish church dedicated to St John the Baptist; used colloquially alongside Perth until the mid-17th century.

historical_names.name: Bertha
historical_names.source: Roman Flavian fort at Bertha (late 1st century AD, confluence of Almond and Tay); associated with Ptolemy's Orrea (c. 150 AD)
historical_names.notes: Bertha was the Roman and early medieval predecessor settlement at the Almond-Tay confluence c. 3 km north of modern Perth.

b_coupar_angus.first_mention_attestation: c. 1160 foundation charters of Coupar Angus Abbey by Malcolm IV ('ecclesia de Cupre')

morphemes.translation: Angus (province name distinguishing it from Cupar in Fife)

b_coupar_angus.etymology_analysis: First recorded in Latin charters as Cupre (c. 1160), of uncertain Pictish or Gaelic origin; 'Angus' was later added to distinguish it from Cupar in Fife.

b_crieff.first_mention_attestation: 1218 charter (Perth & Kinross Council / local burgh records)

morphemes.translation: tree (dative of craobh; or crubha 'haunch/shoulder of a hill')

b_crieff.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic Craoibh (dative of craobh, 'tree'), or alternatively crubha ('haunch', referring to the hill slope).

b_aberdeen.first_mention_attestation: 1172 charter (Chart. Inch.) as Aberdon and c. 1180 as Aberden; royal burgh created by David I (1124-1153)
b_aberdeen.etymology_analysis: From Pictish aber ('river mouth') and the Celtic river name Don/Devona ('mouth of the River Don', originally referring to Old Aberdeen).

b_kincardine.first_mention_attestation: 12th century (royal castle and burgh in The Mearns under William the Lion)
b_kincardine.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Gaelic-Pictish toponym from Gaelic cenn ('head, end') and Pictish *cardden ('thicket, copse', cf. Welsh cardden), meaning 'end of the thicket'; served as the medieval county town of The Mearns (Kincardineshire).

b_ballater.first_mention_attestation: 1696 Poll Book of Aberdeenshire (settlement developed as a spa town c. 1770)
b_ballater.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic Bealadair, usually interpreted as 'pass of the oak/water' or 'town on the sloping hillside' (bealach + leitir/dair), taking its name from the Pass of Ballater.

b_stirling.first_mention_attestation: 1124-1127 royal burgh foundation by David I ('Strivelin')
b_stirling.etymology_analysis: Early forms Strivelin(g) / Stirveling; Thomas Owen Clancy (2017) derives it from Gaelic srib-linn ('pool in the river'), though earlier scholars proposed a Brittonic origin.

historical_names.name: Urbs Giudi
historical_names.source: Bede, Historia Ecclesiastica Gentis Anglorum (731 AD)
historical_names.notes: Most modern scholars identify Bede's 8th-century 'urbs Giudi' with Stirling, though some uncertainty remains.

b_callander.first_mention_attestation: First recorded as Callander in 1238 (and Kallandrech in 1438)
b_callander.etymology_analysis: Uncertain origin: either Brittonic *caleto-dubro- ('hard water', a Calder-type river name) or Gaelic calasraid ('ferry-street' / 'harbour-street'), possibly transferred from Callendar near Falkirk.

b_clackmannan.etymology_analysis: From Gaelic clach (or Brittonic *clog, 'stone/rock') and Manau (genitive Manann), the early medieval Brittonic region at the head of the Firth of Forth; means 'stone of Manau'.

b_annan.first_mention_attestation: 1124 charter recording 'Estrahanent' (Annan valley); 12th-century Bruce motte and castle of 'Anantis'

morphemes.translation: river name (possibly 'she who enriches' or related to Celtic deity Anu)

b_annan.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the River Annan, an ancient Brittonic/Cumbric hydronym (recorded in Estrahanent, 1124).

b_dumfries.first_mention_attestation: Mid-12th century charter as 'Dronfres'; Royal Burgh charter 1186 ('Dunfres' 1189)
b_dumfries.etymology_analysis: From Gaelic Dùn Phris ('fort of the thicket') or Dron/Druim Phris ('ridge of the thicket'), with the second element cognate with Cumbric prēs ('brushwood').

b_kyle.first_mention_attestation: Continuation of Bede (750 AD: 'Eadberctus campum Cyil cum aliis regionibus suo regno addidit')

morphemes.translation: district name (traditionally linked to Coel Hen, or Gaelic coille 'wood' / cùil 'nook')

b_kyle.etymology_analysis: Ancient comital district of Ayrshire, first recorded as campus Cyil in 750 AD; traditionally associated with the legendary Brittonic king Coel Hen.

b_strathgryte.etymology_analysis: From Gaelic Srath Ghriobhaidh ('strath/valley of the River Gryffe'), recorded as Stragrif in 1169; 'Strathgryte' is a scribal variant of Strathgryfe.

b_cunningham.etymology_analysis: Historic Ayrshire district first recorded as Cunegan in 1153, of uncertain Celtic origin (possibly Gaelic coineagan), later assimilated to the Old English/Scots suffix -ham ('homestead').

b_maybole.first_mention_attestation: 1193 charter granted by Donnchadh, Earl of Carrick
b_maybole.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1193; likely from Gaelic magh-baile ('plain-settlement') or Cumbric/Gaelic elements meaning 'heath-pool' (early forms Minnibole).

b_girvan.first_mention_attestation: 1328 traditional charter of Robert the Bruce (burgh of barony charter as 'Garvan' in 1668)
b_girvan.etymology_analysis: Named after the River Girvan, from Brythonic *gwyrdd-afon ('green river') or Gaelic garbh-abhainn ('rough river').

eponym.details: Named after Saint Cuthbert of Lindisfarne (c. 634-687 AD).

b_kilcudbrite.etymology_analysis: From Gaelic Cille Chùithbeirt ('chapel of Cuthbert'), early rendered Kilcudbrit; later Norse-Gaelic influence replaced cill with kirk to produce Kirkcudbright.

b_sanquhar.first_mention_attestation: c. 1213 grant of timber from the forest of Sanquhar by Walter Stewart to Paisley Priory
b_sanquhar.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic An t-Seanchair (sean + cathair), meaning 'the old fort'.

b_wigtown.first_mention_attestation: Sheriffdom of Wigtown attested by 1263 (Largs campaign); burgh mentioned in 1292 indenture
b_wigtown.etymology_analysis: From Old English wīc-tūn ('dwelling place') or Wicga's tūn ('Wicga's farm'), or possibly Old Norse vík ('bay') + Old English tūn ('town on the bay').

b_dumbarton.first_mention_attestation: 1222 royal burgh charter of Alexander II (Gaelic Dùn Breatann)
b_dumbarton.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic Dùn Breatann ('fort of the Britons'), which replaced the earlier Cumbric name Alcluith / Alt Clut in the High Middle Ages.

historical_names.name: Alcluith
historical_names.source: St Patrick's Letter to Coroticus (late 5th century) and Annals of Ulster (658 AD: 'Guret rex Alo Cluathe')
historical_names.notes: Cumbric Alt Clut / Alcluith ('Rock of the Clyde') was the capital of the Kingdom of Strathclyde until its sack in 870 AD.

historical_names.name: Alt Clut
historical_names.source: St Patrick's Letter to Coroticus (late 5th century) and Annals of Ulster (658 AD: 'Guret rex Alo Cluathe')
historical_names.notes: Cumbric Alt Clut / Alcluith ('Rock of the Clyde') was the capital of the Kingdom of Strathclyde until its sack in 870 AD.

b_glasgow.etymology_analysis: From Cumbric *glas-cöü ('green hollow', Gaelic Glaschu), first attested as Glasgu in 1116.

b_meneith.first_mention_attestation: 1164 charter recording Gille Críst, Earl of Menteith
b_meneith.etymology_analysis: From a Brittonic cognate of Welsh mynydd ('moor/upland') combined with the river name Teith ('moor of the Teith').

b_dunbar.first_mention_attestation: Vita Sancti Wilfrithi (c. 710-720, referring to St Wilfrid's imprisonment at 'Dynbaer' in 680 AD)
b_dunbar.etymology_analysis: From Cumbric din-bar ('summit fort'), attested as Dynbaer in the 7th/8th-century Vita Sancti Wilfrithi and later Gaelicised as Dùn Barra.

b_berwick.etymology_analysis: From Old English bere-wīc ('barley farm' or 'outlying grain-farm of a manor'), first recorded as Berewich in 1167.

b_lanark.first_mention_attestation: 978 AD council held by King Kenneth II; made a Royal Burgh by David I in 1140
b_lanark.etymology_analysis: From Cumbric/Brittonic lanerc ('clear space, glade'; cf. Welsh llannerch).

b_cadyou.first_mention_attestation: 1139 royal charters of David I issued at Cadzow (Middle Scots Cadȝow / Cadyou)
b_cadyou.etymology_analysis: Pre-1455 name of Hamilton (Middle Scots Cadȝow, pronounced 'Cadyou', with the letter yogh); a Brittonic/Strathclyde name attested in David I's charters from 1139.

b_biggar.first_mention_attestation: c. 1160 grant of Biggar by Malcolm IV to Baldwin of Biggar; 'Bigir' in 1164 parish records
b_biggar.etymology_analysis: First attested c. 1160 (Bigir 1164); the name is of Celtic (Gaelic or Cumbric) origin, though its exact etymology is uncertain.

b_linlithgow.etymology_analysis: From Cumbric/Old Welsh lynn llaith cau ('lake in the moist hollow'), originally referring to Linlithgow Loch itself.

b_queensferry.first_mention_attestation: Mid-12th century source mentioning 'Portus Regine' (later 'Passagium Sancte Margarete Regine')

eponym.details: Named after Saint Margaret of Scotland (c. 1045-1093), Queen consort of King Malcolm III, who established the ferry across the Firth of Forth for pilgrims.

b_queensferry.etymology_analysis: English/Scots translation of Medieval Latin Portus Regine / Passagium Regine ('the Queen's Ferry'), named for Queen Margaret (d. 1093).

b_falkirk.first_mention_attestation: 1390 Exchequer Rolls ('Faukirk'); earlier recorded as 'Egglesbreth' (c. 1080) and 'Varia Capella' (1166)
b_falkirk.etymology_analysis: Scots calque (Fawkirk, later anglicised to Falkirk) of Gaelic An Eaglais Bhreac / Brittonic Egglesbreth ('speckled church', Latin Varia Capella).

b_edinburgh.first_mention_attestation: Early 12th-century charters of David I (c. 1124-1128; 'Edinburg' 1159); earlier 'oppidum Eden' (954-962) and 'Din Eidyn' (c. 600/638)
b_edinburgh.etymology_analysis: Partial translation of Cumbric Din Eidyn ('fort of Eidyn'), in which Northumbrian Old English/Scots speakers replaced din ('fort') with burh ('fortress/burgh').

historical_names.name: Din Eidyn
historical_names.source: Y Gododdin (c. 600 AD) and Annals of Ulster (638 AD siege of Etin)
historical_names.notes: Din Eidyn was the Cumbric stronghold on Castle Rock before Northumbrian Old English/Scots replaced 'din' with 'burh'.

b_haddington.first_mention_attestation: 1139 charter of King David I granting a toft 'in burgo meo de Hadintun' to the monks of St Andrews

eponym.details: Named after an unrecorded 6th-7th century Anglo-Saxon leader Hadda (OE personal name Hadda + -inga- + tun)

b_haddington.etymology_analysis: Old English *Haddingatūn*, meaning 'farmstead/settlement of Hadda's people', dating linguistically to the 6th-7th century Bernician settlement of Lothian, though first documented as 'Hadintun' in 1139.

b_galashiels.first_mention_attestation: 1416 record of a dispute between the Abbot of Melrose and the laird of Galashiels

morphemes.translation: huts, temporary shelters (from OE *scēla / ON skáli)

b_galashiels.etymology_analysis: Compound of the river name Gala (Gala Water) and Scots 'shiels' (sheilings, huts or shelters by the river), first attested in the early 15th century (1416).

b_penicuick.first_mention_attestation: 1296 entry in Thomas Rymer's Foedera mentioning 'Walter Edgar a person of Penicok south of Edenburgh'
b_penicuick.etymology_analysis: From Brittonic *Pen-y-cog ('hill of the cuckoo'), surviving into Scottish Gaelic as Ceann na Cuthaige; first recorded as 'Penicok' in 1296.

b_kelso.first_mention_attestation: 1128 foundation of Kelso Abbey, where the settlement is recorded as 'Calkou'

morphemes.translation: heel, spur of land, outcrop (Scots heugh)

b_kelso.etymology_analysis: From Old English *calc-hōh ('chalky outcrop/hill-spur'), recorded as 'Calkou' in 1128 (echoed in modern Chalkheugh Terrace). A speculative identification with the Brittonic kingdom/region Calchfynydd lacks contemporary <=867 attestation.

b_jedburgh.first_mention_attestation: Bishop Ecgred of Lindisfarne (r. 830-845 AD) founded two vills named 'Gedwearde' (recorded in Historia de Sancto Cuthberto and Symeon of Durham)
b_jedburgh.etymology_analysis: Originally Old English *Gedwearde / *Gedworð ('enclosed settlement on the River Jed'), founded under Bishop Ecgred of Lindisfarne (830-845 AD); '-burgh' later replaced '-worth', though 'Jeddart/Jethart' preserves the earlier form.

b_selkirk.first_mention_attestation: 1113 charter of Earl David (later King David I) granting lands at Selkirk ('Selechirche') to Tironensian monks
b_selkirk.etymology_analysis: From Old English *sele-cirice ('church by the hall/manor'), attested from c. 1113 in charters of David I.

b_banff.first_mention_attestation: 12th-century Gaelic notitiae in the Book of Deer ('Banb') and 1163 charter of King Malcolm IV

morphemes.translation: uncertain; possibly 'holy woman' (bean-naomh) or 'piglet' (banbh), or related to Banbha

b_banff.etymology_analysis: Recorded as 'Banb' in the 12th-century Book of Deer; W. J. Watson and others link it to Gaelic *bean-naomh* ('holy woman', reflected in the burgh's Virgin Mary arms) or *Banbha*, rather than *banbh* ('piglet').

b_mortlach.first_mention_attestation: 1157 papal bull of Adrian IV and 12th-century Aberdeen episcopal records ('Morthlach' / 'Murthlacum')
b_mortlach.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic *Mòrthlach*, denoting a large hollow or hillock. Although a Class II Pictish stone and tradition of St Moluag (c. 566) exist at the church site, the name itself is first reliably documented in the 12th century.

b_peterhead.first_mention_attestation: 1593 foundation of the planned burgh by George Keith, 5th Earl Marischal (previously 'Peterugie' / 'Inverugie of St Peter' in 1560)

eponym.details: Named after Saint Peter (biblical apostle, 1st century AD), patron saint of the parish church, combined with 'head' (promontory)

b_peterhead.etymology_analysis: Founded in 1593 as a planned fishing port on the headland ('head') of the parish dedicated to St Peter; earlier 1560 grants call the site 'Peterugie' or 'Inverugie of St Peter'.

b_thurso.first_mention_attestation: 12th-century Old Norse sagas (Orkneyinga saga, compiled c. 1200, referring to 11th-12th century events at 'Þjórsá' / 'Thorsa')

morphemes.translation: bull (translating Celtic *tarvos) or the god Thor

b_thurso.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse *Þjórsá* ('bull river', likely a Norse translation of an earlier Celtic *Tarvodubron* 'bull water', or reinterpreted as 'Thor's river'), anglicized as Thurso. First documented in Norse saga traditions of the 12th century.

b_wick.first_mention_attestation: 12th-century Old Norse sagas (Orkneyinga saga, 'Vík') and 12th-century charters
b_wick.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse *vík* ('bay, inlet'), referring to Wick Bay. Although 8th-century Christian missions (St Fergus) and Viking activity occurred in the area, the Norse name 'Wick' is first attested in 12th-century saga and charter sources.

b_inverness.first_mention_attestation: Mid-12th century charters of King David I (c. 1140-1160) granting burgh status to 'Invernis'

morphemes.translation: River Ness (attested as 'Nesa' in Adomnán c. 700)

b_inverness.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic *Inbhir Nis* ('mouth of the River Ness'). While Adomnán's *Vita Columbae* (c. 700) attests the River Ness (*Nesa*) and King Bridei's fortress nearby, the settlement name 'Inverness' (*Invernis*) is first documented in 12th-century charters of David I.

b_badenoch.first_mention_attestation: c. 1229 grant of the Lordship of Badenoch ('Badenach') to Clan Comyn, recorded in the Registrum Episcopatus Moraviensis
b_badenoch.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic *Bàideanach* ('the drowned land'), referring to the floodplains of the upper River Spey and Insh Marshes. First recorded as 'Badenach' c. 1229.

b_glenfinnan.first_mention_attestation: 1745 Jacobite rising records (19 August 1745 raising of the Jacobite standard at Glenfinnan)

eponym.details: Named after the River Finnan (or St Finnan, 6th/7th-century saint)

morphemes.translation: genitive of Fionnan (River Finnan / St Finnan)

b_glenfinnan.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic *Gleann Fhionnain* ('glen of the Finnan' or 'St Finnan's glen'), only entering prominent historical record in the 18th century (1745 Jacobite rising).

b_urquhart.first_mention_attestation: Adomnán's Vita Columbae (c. 700 AD), recording St Columba's 6th-century visit to Emchath at 'Airdchartdan'
b_urquhart.etymology_analysis: Derived from the 7th-century form *Airdchartdan* attested in Adomnán's *Vita Columbae*, a hybrid of Old Irish *aird* ('point/promontory') and Brittonic/Pictish *cardden* ('thicket/wood'), later evolving to Urquhart.

b_glenelg.first_mention_attestation: 1282 charter noting that Glenelg had 'formerly belonged to the King of Man'

morphemes.translation: genitive of Ealg (poetic name for Ireland, or 'noble/worthy')

b_glenelg.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic *Gleann Eilg*, containing *gleann* ('valley') and *Eilg* (poetic Gaelic name for Ireland or 'noble'). First attested in a charter of 1282.

b_elgin.first_mention_attestation: 1151 charter of King David I granting an annuity from Elgin to the Priory of Urquhart (also Cartulary of Moray, 1190)
b_elgin.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic *Eilginn*, probably from *ealg* ('Ireland', 'worthy') or *àille* ('beauty') with diminutive *-inn*. First recorded in a charter of David I in 1151.

b_keith.first_mention_attestation: c. 1180 records of Old Town of Keith ('Kethmalruff', dedicated to St Maol Rubha)
b_keith.etymology_analysis: From a Brittonic/Pictish word meaning 'wood' (cognate with Welsh *coed*), or linked to the Pictish province *Cé*. First documented c. 1180 as 'Kethmalruff' (reflecting an earlier dedication to St Maol Rubha, d. 722).

b_garioch.first_mention_attestation: 1178-1182 charter of King William the Lion granting 'Garviach' to David, Earl of Huntingdon
b_garioch.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic *Gairbheach* ('place of roughness'), first attested as 'Garviach' in a royal charter dated 1178-1182.

b_dingwall.first_mention_attestation: 1226 royal burgh charter of King Alexander II erecting 'Dingwell in Ros'
b_dingwall.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse *Þingvǫllr* ('assembly field'), marking a Viking-Age Norse assembly site, though first entering the written historical record in Alexander II's burgh charter of 1226.

b_gairloch.first_mention_attestation: 1366 charter of William, Earl of Ross, granting Gairloch to Paul McTyre
b_gairloch.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic *Geàrrloch* ('short loch'), referring to Loch Gairloch; first attested in charter records in 1366.

b_tain.first_mention_attestation: 1066 royal charter traditionally attributed to King Malcolm III confirming Tain as a sanctuary and royal burgh
b_tain.etymology_analysis: Derived from the nearby River Tain (from an Indo-European/Celtic root meaning 'flow'). Its Gaelic name *Baile Dhubhthaich* ('Duthac's town') honours St Duthac (d. 1065). First attested in 1066.

b_applecross.first_mention_attestation: 673 AD entry in the Annals of Ulster and Annals of Tigernach recording St Máel Ruba's foundation of 'Apor Crosan'
b_applecross.etymology_analysis: Anglicization (by folk etymology) of Pictish *Aporcrosan* ('confluence of the River Crossan'), attested in the Irish Annals from 673 AD (also 722, 802 AD). Modern Gaelic name is *A' Chomraich* ('The Sanctuary').

b_dornoch.first_mention_attestation: Early 12th-century Dunfermline Abbey register (reign of David I, 1124-1153) ordering Earl Rognvald of Orkney to respect the monks at Dornoch
b_dornoch.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic *Dòrnach* ('pebbly place', i.e. stones the size of a fist). Although archaeological evidence shows 8th-11th century activity, the name is first documented in the early 12th century.

b_durness.first_mention_attestation: 13th-century medieval bishopric of Caithness and Norse saga references ('Dyrnes')
b_durness.etymology_analysis: Likely from Old Norse *Dýrnes* ('deer headland'), or Old Norse *-nes* appended to Gaelic *Dubh Rinn* ('black promontory'). Attested from the 13th century.

b_assynt.first_mention_attestation: c. 1343 royal charter of King David II granting the Barony of Assynt to Torquil MacLeod ('Torkyll M'Cloyd')
b_assynt.etymology_analysis: Probably from Old Norse *Ásendi* ('ridge end', Gaelicized as *Asainn* / *Asainte*), first documented in a royal charter of c. 1343.

b_castletown.first_mention_attestation: 1265 mention of Castle Rushen (Castletown grew around Castle Rushen, first attested by name in the late medieval period)
b_castletown.etymology_analysis: English 'Castletown' (Manx *Balley y Chashtal*), named after Castle Rushen (built/first mentioned 1265), replacing the older district/town name *Rushen* (*Russin*).

b_ramsey.first_mention_attestation: 13th-century Chronicles of Mann (recording 1079 and 1154 landings at Ramsey / 'Hramsa')
b_ramsey.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse *Hramsá* ('wild garlic river', Manx *Rhumsaa*), first recorded in the 13th-century *Chronicles of Mann* in accounts of 11th-12th century Norse rulers.

b_kilmarten.first_mention_attestation: 14th-15th century Argyll medieval church and Campbell/MacTavish records ('Kilmartine')

eponym.details: Named after Saint Martin of Tours (4th-century bishop)

b_kilmarten.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic *Cille Mhàrtainn* ('church of Saint Martin'). While 9th-10th century carved crosses survive at the church and nearby Dunadd is attested in 683 AD, the name 'Kilmartin' is only documented from the late medieval period.

historical_names.name: Dunadd
historical_names.source: Annals of Ulster (683 AD, 'obsessio Duin Att')
historical_names.notes: Dunadd Fort, 5.5 km away in Kilmartin Glen, was the royal capital of Dal Riata and is attested in 683 AD.

historical_names.name: Dunatt
historical_names.source: Annals of Ulster (683 AD, 'obsessio Duin Att')
historical_names.notes: Dunadd Fort, 5.5 km away in Kilmartin Glen, was the royal capital of Dal Riata and is attested in 683 AD.

morphemes.translation: River Coe (meaning uncertain; possibly personal name Comhan)

b_glencoe.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic *Gleann Comhann* ('glen of the River Coe'). The river name *Comhann* may predate Gaelic, though the settlement/glen name is first attested in the 14th century.

b_lomond.first_mention_attestation: c. 828-830 AD Historia Brittonum (Mirabilia Britanniae, 'stagnum Lumonoy')

morphemes.translation: beacon (cf. Early Welsh llumon, 'beacon', referring to Ben Lomond)

b_lomond.etymology_analysis: Attested as *stagnum Lumonoy* in the 9th-century *Historia Brittonum* (c. 828-830), deriving from Brittonic *llumon* ('beacon', reflected in Gaelic *Laomainn* for Ben Lomond / Loch Lomond).

b_ardnamurchon.first_mention_attestation: Adomnán's Vita Columbae (c. 700 AD), recording St Columba's 6th-century visits to 'Artda Muirchol'
b_ardnamurchon.etymology_analysis: Attested as *Artda Muirchol* in Adomnán's *Vita Columbae* (c. 700 AD), meaning 'headland of the sea-hounds' (modern Gaelic *Àird nam Murchan*, anglicized as Ardnamurchan/Ardnamurchon).

b_islay.first_mention_attestation: Adomnán's Vita Columbae (c. 700 AD, 'Ilea'); also early Irish annals ('Ile') and Old Norse ('Íl')

morphemes.translation: island name of unknown pre-Gaelic origin

b_islay.etymology_analysis: Attested as *Ilea* in Adomnán's *Vita Columbae* (c. 700 AD), *Ile* in early Irish records, and *Íl* in Old Norse; the root is pre-Gaelic and of unknown origin.

b_arran.first_mention_attestation: 13th-century Middle Irish poem Agallamh na Senórach ('Arainn') and Norse sagas ('Herrey')

morphemes.translation: possibly 'high place' (cf. Middle Welsh aran) or 'kidney-shaped'

b_arran.etymology_analysis: Scottish Gaelic *Eilean Arainn*; scholars debate a Brittonic derivation (*aran*, 'high place') versus Gaelic *Árainn*. First attested in the 13th-century *Agallamh na Senórach*.

b_mull.first_mention_attestation: c. 150 AD Ptolemy's Geography ('Maleos' / 'Malaios'), and c. 700 AD Adomnán's Vita Columbae ('Malea')
b_mull.etymology_analysis: Attested as *Maleos* in Ptolemy (2nd century AD) and *Malea* in Adomnán's *Vita Columbae* (c. 700 AD), yielding Scottish Gaelic *Muile* and English *Mull*.

historical_names.name: Iona
historical_names.source: Adomnán's Vita Columbae (c. 700 AD, 'Ioua insula', founded 563 AD)
historical_names.notes: For the church holding of Mull (b_mull), Iona (Ioua) just off the southwest coast of Mull was the preeminent ecclesiastical centre from 563 AD.

historical_names.name: Ioua
historical_names.source: Adomnán's Vita Columbae (c. 700 AD, 'Ioua insula', founded 563 AD)
historical_names.notes: For the church holding of Mull (b_mull), Iona (Ioua) just off the southwest coast of Mull was the preeminent ecclesiastical centre from 563 AD.

b_skye.first_mention_attestation: 668 AD Annals of Ulster ('Scith'), c. 700 AD Adomnán's Vita Columbae ('Scia'), and c. 700 Ravenna Cosmography ('Scitis')

morphemes.translation: possibly 'winged' or 'notched' (Scia / Scith / Old Norse Skíð)

b_skye.etymology_analysis: Attested as *Scith* in the Annals of Ulster (668/701 AD), *Scia* in Adomnán (c. 700), and *Skíð* in Old Norse; likely from a pre-Gaelic or early Celtic root meaning 'winged' or 'notched'.

b_lewis.etymology_analysis: Anglicized from Scottish Gaelic *Leòdhas*, which corresponds to Old Norse *Ljóðhús* ('song house' or 'house of people', possibly a Norse folk-etymological adaptation of a pre-Norse name like *leogach*, 'marshy'). First attested in 13th-century Norse sagas.

b_the_uists.etymology_analysis: From Scottish Gaelic *Uibhist*, corresponding to Old Norse *Ívist* ('abode, dwelling'), likely a Norse adaptation of an older pre-Norse or Gaelic name. First attested in 13th-century Norse sagas (and as 'Ywst' in 1549).
